questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t-2)\,i+({t}^{3}-t)\,j$ for $t\in [1,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j \\  & =i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t+1)\,i-2{t}^{2}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t+1,\,y(t)=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+(-4t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(x-2y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}((x-2y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(t+1-2\cdot (-2{t}^{2}))\cdot 1+(t+1)\cdot (-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t+1+4{t}^{2}-4{t}^{2}-4t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}1-3t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}((x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{t},\,y(t)={e}^{t+1}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t+1})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{3t+1}+{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2y\,dx+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,dy+3z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=\,i+t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=1,\,y(t)=t,\,z(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2y\,dx+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,dy+3z\,dz & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+3z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2t\cdot (0)+\operatorname{ln}⁡1\cdot (1)+3{t}^{2}\cdot (2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}6{t}^{2}\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\pi ]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}\cdot (1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{3}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}z\,dx+y\,dy-x\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)={t}^{2},\,z(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}z\,dx+y\,dy-x\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}z\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(z\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{t}^{2}\cdot (2t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{t}^{3}-9{sin}^{2}⁡t-9{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{t}^{3}-9\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the line $r(t)=t\,i+2t\,j+3t\,k$ for $t\in [0,5]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=2t,\,z(t)=3t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j+3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}({y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}4{t}^{2}\cdot (1)+t\cdot (2)+3t\cdot (3)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}4{t}^{2}+11t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{\pi }{4}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){|}_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is a portion of the circle parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\pi -0 \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}-\frac{1}{z}\,dx+x\,dy+dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=t,\,z(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-\frac{1}{z}\,dx+x\,dy+dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{z}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\frac{1}{z}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\pi +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -0 \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(t-1)\,j+{e}^{t}\,k$ for $t\in [0,1].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=t-1,\,z(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =i+j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-1)\cdot (1)+t\cdot (1)+{e}^{t}\cdot ({e}^{t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}+2t-1\,dt \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+{t}^{2}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}+1-1)-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{(2x+y+1)}{x}\,dx+dy,$ where $C$ is a portion of the parabola parametrized by $r(t)=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j$ for $t\in [0,2].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)={t}^{2}-1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\,dx+dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2t+{t}^{2}-1+1}{t}+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+t+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+3t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[2t+\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[2(2)+\frac{3}{2}(2)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[4+6] \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
canonical_examples.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in\left[0,1\right].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
canonical_examples.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^3\,\mathrm{d}x + z\,\mathrm{d}y + y\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $\mathbf{r}(t)=2t\,\mathbf{i} + \cos t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in[0,\pi]?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C y\,\mathrm{d}x -x\,\mathrm{d}y ,$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in[0,\pi].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = \cos t, \qquad
y(t) = 3\sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =-3{t|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$
